title: Approach to Elevated Troponin: Focus on Non‑Ischemic Myocardial Injury
summary: Cardiac troponin indicates myocardial injury, not etiology. Distinguish acute MI (ischemic) from acute or chronic non‑ischemic myocardial injury using symptoms, ECG, imaging, and serial troponins. Management targets the underlying cause; routine ACS therapy is not indicated without ischemia. This guide summarizes an evidence‑based, stepwise approach, common etiologies, testing, and treatment pearls.
clinicalQuestion: How should clinicians evaluate and manage elevated troponin when non‑ischemic myocardial injury is suspected?

keyMoments.title: Confirm injury and acuity
keyMoments.body: Use a high‑sensitivity assay with serial testing to confirm a significant rise/fall (acute) versus stable elevation (chronic). Couple with symptoms, ECG, and imaging to classify ischemic vs non‑ischemic patterns [3], [4].

keyMoments.title: Identify non‑ischemic causes rapidly
keyMoments.body: Common etiologies include sepsis, pulmonary embolism, myocarditis, tachyarrhythmias, heart failure, renal dysfunction, and peri‑procedural injury; management is etiology‑specific [8], [9], [11].

keyMoments.title: Avoid automatic ACS therapy
keyMoments.body: Without ischemia, routine dual antiplatelet therapy or urgent catheterization is not indicated; focus on treating the precipitant and optimizing hemodynamics [3], [4].

keyMoments.title: Risk stratify
keyMoments.body: Even non‑ischemic injury portends higher mortality; consider telemetry, echocardiography, and close follow‑up for high‑risk phenotypes (e.g., sepsis, PE, perioperative injury) [3], [6], [9].

keyMoments.title: Communicate precise diagnosis
keyMoments.body: Document as acute or chronic non‑ischemic myocardial injury when ischemia is not the mechanism; reserve MI terminology for ischemic etiologies per Fourth UDMI [3], [4].

sections.title: Stepwise Approach to Elevated Troponin
sections.blurb: A practical, time‑zero to 6‑hour algorithm grounded in UDMI principles.

steps.title: 1) Verify assay and pretest probability
steps.body: Confirm high‑sensitivity cTn assay, reference limits, and analytic variation. **Contextualize pretest probability of ischemia** using history (typical chest pain, exertional triggers), risk factors, and hemodynamics [3], [4].

steps.title: 2) Immediate ECG and symptom screen
steps.body: Look for new ST‑segment/T‑wave changes, Q waves, or arrhythmias. **Symptoms of supply–demand mismatch or non‑cardiac causes (fever, hypoxia, PE symptoms)** guide down‑stream testing [3], [4].

steps.title: 3) Serial troponins to define acuity
steps.body: Repeat at 1–3 hours. **Significant rise/fall = acute injury; stable elevation = chronic injury**. Large deltas support acute processes but do not specify cause [3], [4].

steps.title: 4) Decide ischemic vs non‑ischemic mechanism
steps.body: Ischemic: symptoms/ECG/imaging consistent with supply–demand or plaque rupture. Non‑ischemic: alternative mechanism without ischemia (e.g., myocarditis, sepsis, renal) [3], [4].

steps.title: 5) If non‑ischemic suspected, pivot evaluation
steps.body: Order targeted tests: CBC, CMP, renal function, CRP, TSH as indicated; CXR; **transthoracic echocardiogram** for wall motion/EF/pericardial effusion; D‑dimer/CTPA if PE suspected; **viral testing or cardiac MRI** for myocarditis; consider tox, drug, and procedure history [5], [8], [9], [11].

steps.title: 6) Management focuses on the cause
steps.body: Treat precipitant (e.g., sepsis source control, rate/rhythm control, anticoagulate PE, adjust dialysis). **Avoid routine antiplatelets/anticoagulation or cath** unless ischemia is present [3], [4].

steps.title: 7) Risk stratify and plan follow‑up
steps.body: Non‑ischemic injury confers adverse prognosis. **Admit/monitor** if high risk (hemodynamic instability, dynamic ECG, LV dysfunction). Arrange cardiology follow‑up, repeat troponin only if clinically indicated [3], [6], [9].

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis of Elevated Troponin Without Ischemia
sections.blurb: Common categories, distinguishing features, and initial management priorities.

cards.title: Cardiac inflammatory/infiltrative
items: Myocarditis: viral prodrome, chest pain, diffuse ST‑T changes; consider cardiac MRI; manage with supportive care, HF therapy; avoid strenuous activity [5], [9].
Pericarditis/myopericarditis: pleuritic pain, friction rub, PR depression; NSAID/colchicine if no contraindication [9].
Infiltrative (amyloid, sarcoid): HF with preserved EF, conduction disease; pursue targeted imaging/biopsy pathways [8].

cards.title: Systemic/critical illness
items: Sepsis/SIRS: supply–demand mismatch, microvascular injury; prioritize antibiotics, fluids/vasopressors, source control [8], [9].
Renal dysfunction: chronic elevation common; interpret deltas; optimize dialysis/volume status [8], [11].
Stroke/head trauma: neuro‑cardiac injury; telemetry, BP and autonomic control [8].

cards.title: Pulmonary/vascular
items: Pulmonary embolism: pleuritic pain, hypoxia, RV strain on ECG/echo; anticoagulate per guidelines; consider lysis if massive [8], [9].
Pulmonary hypertension/ARDS: RV strain; treat underlying respiratory failure [8].

cards.title: Arrhythmias and hemodynamic stress
items: Tachyarrhythmias/AF with RVR: troponin rise from demand; rate/rhythm control, correct triggers [8].
Severe anemia, hypotension, hypertension: correct hemodynamics; avoid unnecessary cath if no ischemia [3], [4], [8].

cards.title: Iatrogenic/procedural/toxic
items: Cardiac procedures (ablation, cardioversion), surgery: expect transient elevations; correlate with symptoms/ECG [8].
Chemotherapy, immune therapies: myocarditis or cardiomyopathy; hold culprit agents, involve cardio‑oncology [8], [11].

cards.title: Perioperative (MINS)
items: Myocardial injury after non‑cardiac surgery: elevated troponin without ischemic symptoms; associated with higher mortality; optimize hemodynamics, analgesia, and consider cardiology input [6].
